0958.event: Pyramids at Nuri stands in Nubia, in what is now Sudan, where the kings of Kush built their tombs around 650 years before the common era. The Kushites, the black pharaohs who had once ruled all of Egypt, raised steep sided pyramids at Nuri near their capital Napata. They were not copies of the great pyramids of Giza. They were smaller, sharper, and their own, built by southern hands for southern kings. Masons set capstones over burial chambers cut deep into the rock, and the dead were laid to rest with the goods of two kingdoms. Egypt's glory did not die. It moved south, up the Nile, and built itself again in stone.
0958.announce: The following poem walks among the steep pyramids at dusk: Pyramids at Nuri.
0958.title: Pyramids at Nuri
0958.piece:
Steep and sharp they rose above the Nubian sand,
the pyramids of Kush, raised by a southern hand.
I watched the masons set the final capstone high
at Nuri, where the old kings sleep beneath the sky.
Not copies of the north, but their own design,
sharp against the dusk, stone upon stone in line.
I walked among the tombs as the shadows grew long and deep.
The south remembers what the north forgot to keep.
Two kingdoms in the grave goods, one river running through,
and glory, born again, in a southern hue.

1092.event: The Plague struck Athens in the year 430 before the common era, in the second year of its long war with Sparta. Crowded with refugees behind the city walls, Athens was ripe for sickness. The disease brought burning fever, red eyes, and a thirst no water could quench. Thucydides, the historian, caught it and lived, and wrote down what he saw: the temples filled with the unburied dead, the funeral pyres running out of wood, the laws of burial abandoned. The plague returned again and again over several years. It carried off a great part of the people, including Pericles, the statesman who had led Athens to its height. The city survived the plague, but something in its spirit did not.
1092.announce: A poem of the crowded city and the summer sickness: The Plague.
1092.title: The Plague
1092.piece:
It came with the summer, the sickness, from the crowded ships,
from the refugees packed inside the Long Walls.
I nursed my neighbors through it. I buried two of them myself.
Thucydides wrote it down: the burning head,
the red eyes, the thirst no water touched,
the bodies laid in the temples because the pyres ran out of wood.
Athens buried its dead without rites, without names.
The laws of burial, of decency, of the gods,
all of it went into the plague pits together.
Pericles lost his sons to it. Then Pericles himself.
The city survived. Something in it did not.
